cards.explanation: The Teacher saw a righteous man perishing in his righteousness. He says it right out loud, in the middle of calling his life futile: "A righteous man perishing in his righteousness…" (Ecclesiastes 7:15) Sometimes the Bible just tells you the hard part plainly.

The answer is False. There's no early funeral for the wicked man here. The text says the Teacher saw "…a wicked man living long in his wickedness." (Ecclesiastes 7:15) The righteous man is the one perishing. Two things that don't match up, and the Teacher just says it straight.

The answer is True. "Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?" (Ecclesiastes 7:16) The Teacher is asking a real question there, friends, and he's warning about going too far. I'll be honest, I read that and my hat tilted a little.

The warning is that you could die before your time. The Teacher asks, "Why should you die before your time?" (Ecclesiastes 7:17) That's his question about being excessively wicked or a fool. He doesn't sugarcoat it, and neither will I.

The one who fears God is the one who follows both warnings. "For he who fears God will follow both warnings." (Ecclesiastes 7:18) The Teacher puts it right there at the end of the verse, friends. Fearing God is where he lands.

The answer is True. "Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins." (Ecclesiastes 7:20) The Teacher says it about everybody. And yes, that includes the guy who shows up with the perfect batch of cookies. That's me, and I'm sitting in that boat with all of you.

The word is cursing. The Teacher says, "…or you may hear your servant cursing you." (Ecclesiastes 7:21) That's what you might overhear. Listening to every word is a good way to ruin a perfectly fine afternoon.

The reason is that you have cursed others many times yourself. The Teacher says, "For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others." (Ecclesiastes 7:22) He's saying you know this from your own heart, friends. Gentle, but it lands.

It was beyond him. The Teacher tested all this by wisdom and resolved to be wise, and then he says, "But it was beyond me." (Ecclesiastes 7:23) Wisdom still outran him. I think that's a humble thing to admit.

The answer is True. "What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?" (Ecclesiastes 7:24) Picture reaching down a well and your arm just runs out. That's the feeling the Teacher is putting into words, and he asks the question out loud.

The Teacher also sets his mind to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness. He says he directed his mind "…to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness." (Ecclesiastes 7:25) It sits right beside wisdom and explanations. That's some serious homework.

The man who pleases God is the one who escapes. "The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared." (Ecclesiastes 7:26) The Teacher puts two men side by side, friends. The one who pleases God is the one who gets away.

The word is searching. "While my soul was still searching but not finding…" (Ecclesiastes 7:28) He kept looking even when he wasn't finding. I know a little about waiting around for something to turn up, after all those years in the back of a junk drawer.

Mankind sought out many schemes. The Teacher says, "…God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes." (Ecclesiastes 7:29) That's what he says he found. One thing, and it's about all of us.
